EQUIPMENT REQUIRED
A highly efficient long range mode of voice communication is required by radio amateurs and commercial users.
INTRODUCTIONM
Single sideband systems are more efficient than AM systems because a carrier signal is not transmitted.

In this lesson you will see how the SSB is a more efficient means of signal processing. Also, you will have an understanding of the different transmission lines available for transferring the signal from component to component.
Let's begin the lesson on SINGLE SIDEBAND TRANSMISSION LINES................
LESSON MENU
SINGLE SIDEBAND TRANSMISSION
Remember from previous lessons, the Amplitude Modulated signal contains the upper sideband, carrier and lower sideband.
DISCUSSION
Suppressing one sideband and the carrier before transmission of an Amplitude Modulated signal results in using half the spectrum space. This process is called Single Sideband transmission.
A Single Sideband system is very similar to an AM Modulated system. However, Single Sideband offers the advantage of power efficiency, bandwidth efficiency and eliminates harmonic distortion.
As you know, a carrier signal must be present in the transmitter to produce the sidebands and the receiver needs the carrier to reproduce the original signal.
However, the carrier signals for the transmitter and receiver do not have to be exactly the same carrier. This allows the carrier to be suppressed at the transmitter.
The receiver generates a replacement carrier signal so that the sideband and information may be heterodyned with the carrier.

DEFINITION
In the transmitter, the input audio signal is amplified to the proper level by the audio amplifier and is directed to the Balanced Modulator.
The balanced modulator uses non-linear circuits to suppress the carrier signal. The Carrier signal is suppressed through what is called phase cancellation.
This means when the secondary voltage at T2 becomes positive, the four diodes become reversed biased.
Current flows from audio input (T1) through T3 for the duration of the positive alternation of the carrier signal. This results in an audio signal output during the positive alternation.

When the carrier signal shifts to the negative alteration, the diodes become forward biased and place a short across the primary of T3. This results in a zero output or phase cancellation during the negative alternation.
One complete cycle of the carrier signal has just been explained. However, the audio signal has not completed its full cycle.
This sequence is continued until the audio signal has been fully processed. When no audio signal is present, the output will always be a zero signal.
The carrier signal is never allowed to flow through the primary of T3 and is suppressed in the Balanced Modulator.
Now the upper and lower sidebands are the only output of the balance modulator to the systems bandpass filter.
The bandpass filter will pass the selected band of frequencies (either the high sideband or the low sideband). The unused sideband is then attenuated.
Our example is passing the high sideband. But the low sideband could have been passed with the high sideband attenuated.

An AM transmitter uses 1/3 of the total power for both sidebands. Or 1/6 of the total power per sideband. This means the other 2/3 of the total power is used for the carrier.
Because the single sideband system supresses the carrier and one sideband. The transmitter uses only 1/6 of the total power of the AM transmitter for the same information signal.
Since the Single Sideband signal is narrow compared to an AM signal, the Single Sideband receiver uses an RF Amplifier to amplify the received signal.
The RF Amplifier also sets the receivers sensitivity and keeps the frequency converter from radiating signals back through the receiving antenna.
Since the signal's frequency was increased for transmission, the frequency converter lowers the signal to an intermediate frequency (IF).
The IF Amplifier provides most of the receiver's gain and maintains the optimum bandwidth. This helps preserve the original modulated information.
Unlike the RF Amplifier, the IF Amplifier operates at a lower fixed frequency.
At this point the information is still located on the one sideband. In the AM receiver a demodulator was used to recreate the orignal audio signal from the two sidebands and carrier.
Our signal is only on one sideband minus the carrier. So a Product Demodulator is used to recreate the original audio signal from the single sideband.
The Product Demodulator heterodyned the oscillator's carrier signal to the information signal from the IF amplifier.

TRANSMISSION LINESE
AM, FM or SSB signal processing systems send electrical pulses or signals from component to component.
DISCUSSION
The physical structure that will guide the signal (electromagnetic waves) from place to place is defined as a transmission line.
Transmission lines are conductors or a series of conductors used to form a continuous path from component to component.
Lines used to connect your television set to an antenna or a cable service are transmission lines.

The optimum transmission line is one that provides maximum transfer with minimum loss due to the properties of the line. raphics Text)Line Properties Resistive Loss Induction Loss Radiation Loss Capacitive Loss
4. Difference of the Two Signals (Origianal Audio)
Whenever a conductor transfers energy, the natural resistance of the conductor causes a power loss.
If the line is of any considerable length, this could be a large amount of power loss. This type of loss is referred to as copper loss.
High frequency current has a tendency to flow to the outside of the conductor. This is called skin effect.

As frequency increases the depth of penetration into the conductive surface decreases. The magnetic flux surrounding each moving electron encounters more resistances towards the center of the conductor.
This reduces the effective cross section of the conductor. Meaning the size of the useful part of the conductor is reduced.
Depth of penetration of the current is defined as skin depth. Skin depth is the distance into the conducting medium for which current is reduced.
One way to reduce the loss is to increase the surface area of the conductor. he conductor.
This is why in higher frequency applications a waveguide (hollow conductor) is more effective than a standard wire or cable type conductors for transmission lines.
The second property of transmission lines is induction loss.
Electromagnetic waves are made of electric fields associated with voltage and magnetic fields associated with current flow.

When the magnetic field expands and collapses it induces voltage and current into conducting material near the transmission lines; resulting in a power loss to nearby items. This type of loss is called induction.
One method used to reduce the induction loss is to use standoff insulators between the transmission line and other surfaces. Standoff insulators are used on common television antenna wires.
Radiation loss is similar to induction loss. However, the loss is to the atmosphere and not to a nearby object. This type of loss is desirable in an antenna, but undesirable in a transmission line.
In both induction and radiation, expanding and collapsing the flux field at even faster rates tends to increase the number of flux lines which never return to the inductor.
Placing a shield around the conductor of the transmission line prevents interaction with other circuits. This type of shielding reduces the radiation and induction losses.
On a two wire transmission line, the insulation is the dielectric for the capacitance of the line. Charged and discharged, the electrons of the dielectric (insulation) continuously change.
This type of energy loss is called capacitive loss and is normally in the form of heat dissipation.
The loss is held to a minimum with the use of high resistance dielectric (insulation).
Capacitive loss appears as a resistive loss to the power source and increases as the frequency is increased.

There are several factors to consider when selecting a transmission line. For example; the breakdown voltage, power loss at the required frequency, stability of dielectric, flexibility and cost.
There are many different types of transmission lines used today. In this lesson will discuss four of the most used types.
Anyone who has had cable television service has used a flexible coaxial cable. This type of transmission line is most commonly used in radio, television, microwave and radar services.
The center wire is the conductor and is usually solid. The outer conductor is braided.
The two conductors are separated by a polyethylene plastic.
This type of transmission line has very little radiation loss because the inner conductor is shielded by the outer conductor.
This cable is capable of transferring large amounts of power at high frequencies with only small amounts of skin effect and dielectric loss.
Another type of coaxial cable is the rigid coaxial. Just like the flexible coaxial cable, there is a center and an outer conductor.
However, the outer conductor is a rigid metal tube and has insulating disks to separate the center from the outer conductor.
Similar to the flexible coaxial cable, the rigid coaxial has little radiation loss and is used for large power and frequencies up to 3 GHz.
Another commonly used cable is the twin lead line. This cable is used widely for television reception.
The twin lead line consists of two conductors molded into the edges of a polyethylene strip or ribbon. The polyethylene is solid enough to keep the conductors separated.
This line is still flexible enough to bend around corners..
Because of the small size and distance between the two conductors, the twin lead is used for transmission of low power frequencies up to 200 MHz.

Another type of line can be used for low power transmissions besides the twin lead. It is the Open Two Wire line. It has two bare conductors spaced by insulators. The insulators maintain an even space between the wires.
There are three factors that determine the distance between the two conductors of a open two wire line.
Due to the fact that the conductors are bare with no shielding, the major power loss is due to radiation loss.
The simplest and less expensive transmission line is the twisted pair. Most commonly used for telephone circuits, household appliance and other low frequency purposes.
The twisting of the two wires equalizes the effect of stray fields on both conductors. This type of cable is also used for low voltage and low frequency transmission.

A transmission line can be measured in length electrically and physically.
Electrical length is a comparison of physical length and wavelength. Wavelength is the distance the energy travels down the line during one cycle.
To determine electrical length you must understand frequency wavelength. RF (radio frequency) signals travel at the speed of light, 186,000 miles per second.
However, the transmission line has inductance and shunt capacitance. This slows the RF signal down.
Because different types of lines have different characteristics the effect they have on RF signal speed (velocity) is different.
To determine the frequency wavelength of a 60 MHz signal through a twisted pair line that is rated at 60% speed of light, divide the velocity by the frequency.
Now that we have the frequency length, the electrical length can be determined. Divide the physical length by the frequency length will result in the electrical length.
As you can see the type of transmission line used plays an important role in signal transmission and reception. Remember that all line characteristics need to be considered for good communication.
